summary:
Colorado's Anti-Discrimination Act prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity and gender expression in employment, housing, public accommodations, education and credit, a coverage in force since 2008 and expanded again by the 2025 legislature, as documented in the Colorado Legislature's own 2025 summary of gender-affirming-care and transgender legislation. As of 12 October 2026 the state's gender-identity policy score stands at 23.25 of 25 within an overall score of 44.5 of 47, and a July 2026 national legal-risk assessment lists Colorado among the most protective states for transgender people.

House Bill 1312, the Kelly Loving Act, was signed by Governor Jared Polis on 16 May 2025 after passing on 6 May. It requires employers and schools to use a person's chosen name and pronouns, prohibits deadnaming and misgendering in workplaces and schools with immediate effect, and requires schools with dress codes to allow a student to choose from any uniform option. Its provisions simplifying changes of gender identity on birth certificates and driver's licences, and changes of name on marriage licences, take effect on 1 October 2026.

Gender markers on state documents are changeable without surgery. The Board of the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment removed the surgical requirement unanimously in February 2019, ending a rule that had applied since 1 January 1984. A change is made by request, using a Change of Sex Designation form to the Division of Motor Vehicles for licences and IDs and Birth Certificate Correction and Sex Designation forms to the Department of Health for birth certificates. Birth certificates offer M, F, Intersex and X markers; IDs and licences offer male, female and X. Minors need parent or guardian consent plus confirmation from a medical or mental health professional.

Facilities access is protected. In 2013 the Colorado Civil Rights Division ruled that transgender six-year-old Coy Mathis could use the girls' restroom at her elementary school in Fountain, and in 2023 Colorado implemented a law granting full access to bathroom facilities for all genders. The state anti-bullying law prohibits bullying on the basis of gender identity and requires school districts to adopt prevention policies.

Colorado's hate-crime law has covered gender identity or expression since 2001, with penalty enhancements for bias-motivated crimes. In 2009 a Greeley jury convicted a man of first-degree murder with a hate-crime finding in a case described as the first murder trial applying a hate-crime law where the victim was transgender. The gay panic defence was abolished by a bipartisan bill passed in June 2020 and signed in July 2020, effective immediately.

Gender-affirming care is protected at state level but is under direct pressure. Legislation signed in April 2023 was enacted to protect, defend and guarantee gender-affirming healthcare services and to guarantee safe passage of transgender individuals from other states. Since the beginning of 2023 basic health insurance coverage in Colorado must explicitly include sexual reassignment surgery as a basic policy, and a July 2026 assessment counts Colorado among the states with comprehensive health-insurance laws covering facial-hair removal and expanded gender-related coverage. On 18 May 2026 the Colorado Supreme Court ruled 5-2 that Children's Hospital Colorado violated state anti-discrimination law when it suspended gender-affirming care for transgender youth under federal pressure, and ordered a lower court to issue an injunction requiring the hospital to resume puberty blockers and hormone therapy. Justice William Hood wrote that continuing such treatment for cisgender children while stopping it for transgender youth meant the decision denies the petitioners the full and equal enjoyment of services based on gender identity; two justices dissented, citing federal threats that could shut the hospital system.

Conversion therapy has been banned statewide on minors since a bill signed on 31 May 2019. After the Colorado Supreme Court's 8-1 ruling of 31 March 2026 in Chiles v. Salazar requiring strict scrutiny of that ban, House Bill 26-1322, passed on 8 May 2026, redefines conversion therapy as direction toward a pre-determined gender identity or sexual orientation outcome and removes the statute of limitations for claims.

Custody is governed by litigation rather than statute. A 2019 class action on behalf of transgender women held in men's prisons alleged that the Colorado Department of Corrections subjected them to sexual and physical violence and denied medically necessary care. The court-approved 2024 consent decree in Raven v. Polis, entered in Denver District Court, required the department to expand health care, create voluntary specialised housing comprising a 100-bed unit at the men's Sterling facility and an integration unit at the women's prison, and pay about $2.1 million to roughly 400 class members without admitting liability. A separate 2019 settlement paid Lindsay Saunders-Velez $170,000 over the safety of a transgender inmate held in a men's prison. No identity-based-housing statute governs placement in Colorado; trans women were historically held in men's prisons, with relief won through consent decree rather than a baseline housing rule.
tangentialFactors:
Three ballot measures certified for the November 2026 vote would, if passed, write restrictions on transgender minors into Colorado law. Initiative 109 would ban transgender children from gendered sports that do not align with their biological sex, and Initiative 110 would prohibit surgery on a child for the purpose of altering their sex characteristics; a third certified measure, Initiative 108, concerns child sex trafficking. The measures were pushed by conservative activists and signatures were certified by state elections officials on 17 March 2026.

Restrictions on transgender students in school sport have been adopted at district level. In April 2025 the D49 school board voted 3-2 to advance a policy banning biologically male students from female sports and the reverse; the D-11 Board voted 6-1 in June 2025 for a similar policy, with Academy District 20 following suit. In December 2025 an undisclosed lawsuit settlement was reached over the banning of trans individuals from playing on female sports teams within some association governing districts, and the terms of that settlement are not public.

Colorado's protective framework is operating under direct national funding pressure. The state's own Medicaid agency has said that restoring coverage suspended under a federal rule will require legislative action, which indicates that state-level protection does not by itself hold when national funding conditions change. A visitor assessing Colorado should read its protections together with that constraint rather than as a fixed ceiling on what the state can deliver.
localsOnly:
Colorado will suspend Medicaid coverage for hormone therapy, puberty blockers and other gender-affirming care for transgender youth beginning 13 October 2026, because a national rule finalised in August 2026 blocks federal funds for such care for people under 18, and under 19 under the CHP+ child programme. The state's Medicaid agency said resuming coverage will require legislative action. About 500 youth under 19 received Medicaid-covered hormone therapy for gender dysphoria in fiscal 2024-25. Patients already taking hormones keep coverage through a six-month tapering period, and behavioural healthcare is unaffected.

The state anti-bullying law requires school districts to adopt prevention policies covering bullying on the basis of gender identity, and schools with dress codes must allow any uniform option under the Kelly Loving Act. These are resident-facing obligations on Colorado school districts rather than rules a visitor would encounter.

Implementation of the Kelly Loving Act's document provisions is dated 1 October 2026, so changes of gender identity on Colorado birth certificates and driver's licences and changes of name on marriage licences made before that date proceed under the earlier procedures.
outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the November 2026 ballot measures is unresolved; Initiative 109 and Initiative 110 were certified for the vote but their passage and any subsequent litigation are not sourced here.

The terms of the December 2025 lawsuit settlement concerning trans individuals barred from female sports teams in some association governing districts are undisclosed in the sources, so which districts are bound and on what terms remains unresolved.

Compliance with the 18 May 2026 Colorado Supreme Court order is not sourced beyond the direction to a lower court to issue an injunction; whether Children's Hospital Colorado resumed puberty blockers and hormone therapy, and whether other Colorado hospitals altered care under federal pressure, is unresolved.

Whether the Kelly Loving Act's document-change provisions are operating as written after their 1 October 2026 effective date is not documented in the sources.

The status of the conversion-therapy regime after House Bill 26-1322, including any challenge to the redefined statute or to the strict-scrutiny standard set in Chiles v. Salazar, is unresolved.

No Colorado-specific figure for killings or violence against transgender people, measured against the state's general homicide rate, appears in the sources; no such comparison can be made from this inventory.
